Cause Investigation

The image worker disappeared from the dashboard just after a rollout. The worker’s terminal record is missing. Operations has suggested a memory kill. Walk me through how to distinguish an orchestrator stop from a memory kill, including which records to match and what would leave the cause unresolved.

Baseline · repetition 1 · Automatic pass · 269 words

Blind review · Passed
Identifies the records needed for each cause, qualifies cgroup-level evidence, and explains when independent records can resolve the cause despite the missing terminal record.

**f1** Match the exact worker instance first. Use its immutable workload or allocation ID and container ID to join the rollout history, orchestrator events, container runtime records, and node logs. Match the node and timestamps, accounting for clock skew. If the kernel recorded a PID or cgroup, use runtime metadata to map it back to that container. A replacement can have the same worker name.

**f2** Trace an orchestrator stop from decision to execution. Look for the rollout controller selecting that instance for removal, then a node-agent or runtime record showing it acted on the stop request. A recorded exit after `SIGTERM`, or a recorded `SIGKILL` when the grace period expired, ties the termination to the stop. A deletion request alone establishes intent.

**f3** Trace a memory kill to its victim. Look for a kernel OOM record naming the worker process as the victim, or a runtime `OOMKilled` termination reason for that container. A cgroup `oom_kill` counter increase corroborates a kill in that cgroup. If it contained several processes, identify which one died. A node agent can also evict a worker under memory pressure. That is an orchestrator stop triggered by memory pressure.

**f4** Keep the immediate cause unresolved if the records show only rollout timing, high memory use, dashboard disappearance, or exit code `137`. Both a forced stop and an OOM kill can produce `137`. If a stop was requested and an OOM event also occurred, the victim identity and event order matter. The missing terminal record needn’t prevent attribution if independent records establish what ended the worker. On the evidence given, the memory kill remains a hypothesis.
Candidate · repetition 1 · Automatic pass · 286 words

Blind review · Passed
Traces both causes to the exact worker attempt and explains why event order, victim identity, and the distinction between event time and ingestion time matter.

**f1** The cause is unresolved on the supplied evidence. The dashboard shows when the worker disappeared. The rollout timing and Operations’ memory-kill hypothesis do not establish what terminated it.

**d1** Identify the exact worker attempt. Match its immutable instance or pod UID, container ID, restart attempt, and node across records. Put event timestamps on a common clock and distinguish event time from log ingestion time. A replacement can reuse the worker’s name.

**d2** Trace an orchestrator stop from request to exit. Match the rollout controller’s deletion or scale-down decision to the node agent’s stop request for that container, then to the runtime’s signal and exit records. A graceful exit after `SIGTERM`, or a recorded grace-period expiry followed by a forced kill, supports that sequence. A deletion request alone establishes intent. It can also arrive after the worker has already died.

**d3** Trace a memory kill to its victim. Look for a retained runtime termination reason such as `OOMKilled`, or a node kernel OOM record naming the victim PID. For a kernel record, match the PID and cgroup to the container at the time of death and verify that the victim was the worker process. A node-pressure eviction is an orchestrator stop prompted by memory pressure. A memory graph alone cannot identify who killed the process.

**d4** Reconcile competing records in event order. If the exact worker was OOM-killed during rollout shutdown, report both facts. The rollout initiated shutdown and the OOM kill terminated the worker. Exit code `137` alone cannot distinguish the two because either path can produce `SIGKILL`. If the surviving records show only rollout activity, memory pressure, or an unattributed kill, or cannot distinguish the old attempt from its replacement, leave the cause unresolved.

**f1** Start with the last worker instance seen on the dashboard. Match its worker ID to the orchestrator’s instance or task ID, container ID, restart attempt, and node. Put the rollout, last heartbeat, and recorded events on the same clock. The last heartbeat tells you when visibility ended. A replacement worker with the same name has its own history.

**f2** To establish an orchestrator stop, match a controller or audit record that selected that instance for termination to a node-agent or container-runtime record showing the stop was carried out. For example, the rollout controller requested deletion of the old instance, the node agent sent `SIGTERM`, and the runtime recorded its exit. If the grace period expired, look for the node agent’s recorded escalation to `SIGKILL`. A rollout timestamp alone establishes timing. A deletion request establishes intent.

**f3** To establish a memory kill, look for an `OOMKilled` termination reason on that exact container attempt, or a kernel OOM record naming the victim PID and cgroup. Map the victim back to the worker process on the same node at the time of exit. A memory spike or a node-wide OOM event supports investigating memory pressure. Either can occur while a different process is killed. If the orchestrator recorded a memory-pressure eviction, that establishes an orchestrator decision to stop the instance.

**f4** If both paths appear, report the stop request and the immediate cause of exit separately. A rollout can request termination and the kernel can OOM-kill the worker during its grace period. Exit code `137` alone cannot distinguish that sequence from the node agent enforcing its timeout. You can call it a memory kill only if the kernel or runtime recorded an OOM kill for the exact process that vanished. A rollout timestamp nearby proves nothing either way. Exit code 137 is SIGKILL, which both a grace-period expiry and the OOM killer produce, so the code alone settles nothing.

**l1** Records to collect and match, in order:

**l1i1** First check whether the worker died at all. A rollout replaces instances, so the dashboard may have lost track of a healthy replacement because its pod name, ID or labels changed. Look for a running instance of the new revision before investigating a death.

**l1i2** Identify the old instance. Get its container ID or pod UID, its node, and its main PID from the orchestrator's history, which might be ReplicaSet or task history, the audit log, or the event stream. Every later record has to match this identity. Matching on "the image worker" is not enough.

**l1i3** Get the orchestrator's stop record for that instance. This is the rollout or scale-down decision, followed by a kill or stop event. That event means SIGTERM was sent, then SIGKILL if the grace period ran out. A clean stop exits 143, or 0 if the worker handles SIGTERM. A grace-period expiry exits 137.

**l1i4** Get the kernel OOM record from that node. In `dmesg` or the journal, look for `Memory cgroup out of memory` or `Out of memory: Killed process <pid>`. Its PID and cgroup path must match the worker's. Also check whether the cgroup's `memory.events` `oom_kill` counter went up, and whether the runtime reported `OOMKilled: true` (in Kubernetes, `lastState.terminated.reason`).

**l1i5** Check memory usage just before death. If memory climbed to the limit, that supports an OOM kill. If memory stayed flat and the orchestrator issued a stop just before death, the stop is the likely cause. This metric only supports the other records. It cannot establish the cause by itself.

**l1i6** Put the matched records in order. If both a stop event and an OOM kill exist, whichever happened first killed the process. For example, a worker can hit OOM while draining after SIGTERM. In that case the orchestrator started the shutdown and memory finished it, and the report should say both.

**l2** The cause stays unresolved if any of these apply:

**l2i1** The terminal record and the runtime's container record are both gone. This is likely in your case, because a rollout deletes the old pod object along with its status. If no event or audit log kept a copy elsewhere, you have no exit status to read.

**l2i2** The node's kernel log was not shipped off the node and has since rotated. The same applies if the node itself is gone, for example because an autoscaler terminated it. A node termination would also be a third cause in its own right, separate from both a rollout stop and an OOM kill.

**l2i3** You cannot tie a record to this instance. Examples are an OOM line whose PID or cgroup you cannot map to the worker, or a stop event that names only the deployment and not this instance.

**l2i4** The clocks on different sources disagree by more than the gap between the events you are trying to order.

**l2i5** Metrics are too coarse to show memory at the moment of death. For example, 60-second samples can miss a spike that lasted a few seconds.

If l2i1 and l2i2 both hold, the honest answer is "terminated at roughly the rollout time, cause undetermined." In that case Operations' memory-kill theory is a hypothesis built on timing, not a finding.

- **OOM during drain:** the rollout sent SIGTERM and the worker was OOM-killed while finishing in-flight images. The orchestrator event comes first and the kernel OOM line comes second, both for the same PID.

**l2i2** The node's kernel log is gone. Rotation, a restart, or an autoscaler removing the node all destroy it. Without it you cannot confirm or exclude a kernel OOM.

**l2i3** Records exist but cannot be tied to the worker. For example, an OOM line names a PID you cannot map to this container, or clock skew between hosts puts the stop event and the death time out of order.

**l2i4** Only an exit code survives. A bare 137 with no reason field and no kernel record fits a grace-period SIGKILL as well as an OOM kill.

**l2i5** No record mentions the worker at all. Then you have neither cause. Separately, "disappeared from the dashboard" may only mean the dashboard tracks instance IDs and the replacement registered under a new one. Confirm the worker actually died before explaining why.

**l2i6** Under any of these, report it as "cause undetermined: <which record is missing>". Rollout timing then supports an orchestrator stop only as a hypothesis, and the Operations claim stays a guess.

Cause Investigation

The image worker disappeared from the dashboard just after a rollout. The worker’s terminal record is missing. Operations has suggested a memory kill. Walk me through how to distinguish an orchestrator stop from a memory kill, including which records to match and what would leave the cause unresolved.

Baseline · repetition 1 · Automatic pass · 334 words

Blind review · Passed
It distinguishes dashboard disappearance from process exit, matches each possible cause to the exact attempt, and explains why a cgroup counter or exit 137 alone cannot identify what killed the worker.

**f1** The cause is unresolved. The dashboard establishes when the worker disappeared from view. It does not establish that the process exited. The rollout timing and Operations’ memory-kill hypothesis give you two leads.

**d1** Identify the exact worker attempt. Start with its last heartbeat or registration and recover its task or allocation ID, execution attempt, node, and start time. On Kubernetes, use the pod UID and container ID. Match event timestamps on a common clock so a replacement with the same name, or a reused host PID, doesn’t get mistaken for the missing worker. [Kubernetes pod lifecycle](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/)

**d2** Trace an orchestrator stop from request to exit. Find the controller or audit record that targeted that attempt for removal, then match it to the node agent or runtime record showing the stop was carried out. A worker log acknowledging the shutdown signal followed by a recorded exit supports graceful termination. A runtime record showing the grace period expired and the runtime killed the still-running process supports a forced stop. A delete request alone establishes intent. [Kubernetes pod termination flow](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/#pod-termination-flow)

**d3** Trace a memory kill to its victim. Look for an `OOMKilled` termination reason on that container attempt, or a kernel OOM record naming a victim whose host PID and cgroup map to the worker at that time. An increase in the cgroup’s `oom_kill` counter confirms that an OOM killer killed a process in its scope. If the cgroup held several processes, the counter alone cannot identify which one died. [Linux cgroup memory events](https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/cgroup-v2.html#memory-interface-files)

**f2** Report both events if the records show both. If the controller requested a stop and the kernel then identified the worker as its OOM victim, the rollout initiated shutdown and OOM caused the exit. If all that survives is a stop request, a memory spike, or exit code 137, leave the cause open. Both an enforced stop and an OOM kill can produce `SIGKILL`; code 137 alone identifies no sender. With no worker-specific exit or kill record, even termination remains unconfirmed.

**d2** To establish an orchestrator stop, trace the request to its outcome. Look for a controller or audit record selecting that instance for termination, a node-agent or runtime record delivering the stop, and an exit record consistent with that sequence. A runtime record that the worker exited after `SIGTERM`, or that the runtime killed it when its grace period expired, can supply the missing terminal evidence. **d4** If both trails exist, order the events. A rollout can initiate shutdown and the OOM killer can kill the worker during its grace period. Report both when the records support both. If all you recover is exit code 137 or `SIGKILL`, the sender remains unknown. If the decisive records expired, identify different instances, or cannot establish the sequence, leave the cause unresolved.

Match the container's identity across orchestrator, runtime and kernel records. A memory kill leaves a kernel OOM line naming that container's cgroup. An orchestrator stop leaves a stop or delete decision followed by SIGTERM. Exit code 137 alone proves neither, because a SIGKILL after an expired grace period also produces 137.

**f1** The rollout is the default suspect, not memory. A rollout deliberately terminates old workers, so a worker vanishing "just after" one is expected behaviour until something says otherwise. Operations' memory theory is a hypothesis that needs a kernel record behind it.

**f2** The missing terminal record is probably a consequence of the rollout, not a clue. When the orchestrator deletes the old pod, `lastState.terminated` (reason, exit code, timestamps) disappears with it. Kubernetes events expire after about an hour by default. **l1** Records to collect, keyed to the same container ID or pod UID, not just the same minute:

- **l1i1** Orchestrator events and the rollout timeline. Look for the ReplicaSet scale-down or pod deletion and the `Killing` event for this pod, plus when the new ReplicaSet came up. A stop decision timestamped before the exit points to the orchestrator.
- **l1i2** Termination status, if anything archived it (an event exporter, kube-state-metrics, audit log).
  - `reason: OOMKilled` points to memory.
  - `Completed` or `Error` with exit 143 means SIGTERM was honoured: an orchestrator stop.
  - Exit 137 with no OOM reason means the grace period ran out and it was SIGKILLed. That is still an orchestrator stop.
- **l1i3** Kernel log on the node (`journalctl -k`, `dmesg`, node log shipping). Search for `Memory cgroup out of memory` or `oom-kill:` and check that the `task_memcg` / cgroup path contains this container's ID. This is the decisive record for a memory kill. An OOM line naming a different container on the same node is noise.
- **l1i4** Container runtime events (containerd or CRI-O `TaskOOM` / `oom` event, `TaskExit`) with the container ID. These corroborate l1i3 and give the exact exit timestamp.
- **l1i5** Memory metrics for the container (cAdvisor `container_memory_working_set_bytes` against its limit). A climb to the limit right before exit supports OOM. A flat line ending at the deletion time supports a stop. Treat this as supporting evidence only: scrape intervals can miss a spike.
- **l1i6** The worker's own log tail. A logged SIGTERM handler or shutdown message means the orchestrator asked it to stop. An abrupt end mid-job fits SIGKILL, but SIGKILL can come from either cause.
- **l1i7** Audit log, if enabled. It shows who or what issued the delete (the rollout controller, an HPA, or a human), which settles "orchestrator stop" more firmly than event timing.

**f3** How the records combine:

| ID | Pattern | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| f3i1 | Delete/Killing event → SIGTERM logged → exit 143, no matching kernel OOM line | Orchestrator stop, clean |
| f3i2 | Delete/Killing event → exit 137 roughly `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` later, no OOM line | Orchestrator stop; the worker ignored or overran SIGTERM |
| f3i3 | Kernel OOM line with this container's cgroup, runtime OOM event, memory at limit, no prior delete | Memory kill |
| f3i4 | OOM line for this container *during* the grace period after a delete | Both happened; the memory kill delivered the final blow during shutdown. Worth knowing if shutdown work inflates memory |

**f4** Things that leave the cause unresolved:

- **f4i1** No kernel log retained from that node, especially if the node was drained or recycled in the same rollout. Without it you can't confirm a memory kill, only fail to rule it out.
- **f4i2** Events expired and no exporter or audit log captured the delete. The orchestrator's decision then rests only on the rollout's timing, which is correlation, not a record.
- **f4i3** Exit 137 is the only surviving fact. It fits both f3i2 and f3i3.
- **f4i4** Container IDs can't be matched across sources, for example the kernel line only gives a PID and nothing maps that PID to the container. A time-only match is a hypothesis.
- **f4i5** The worker may not have died at all. A rollout can change labels, the metrics endpoint, or the dashboard query, so a healthy new worker stops appearing. Check that a replacement worker is running and reporting before attributing any death.

If the kernel and runtime records are gone, the honest conclusion is "consistent with a rollout stop, memory kill not excluded." Don't let operations upgrade that to an OOM because 137 looks familiar.

Match records by the worker's container identity, not by how close they are to the rollout. An orchestrator stop leaves a deletion and SIGTERM trail. A memory kill leaves a kernel OOM record for that container's cgroup. Exit code 137 alone proves neither. The examples below use Kubernetes terms; other orchestrators have equivalent records.

**l1** Procedure, in order:

- **l1i1** **Confirm the worker actually died.** A worker missing from the dashboard is not necessarily a dead worker. Check the orchestrator for the container's state and restart count, and check whether the process still exists on the node. If it is alive and has stopped reporting, this is a telemetry problem and the rest of this list doesn't apply.
- **l1i2** **Pin the identity.** Record the pod UID, container ID, node, and the process's host PID from the container runtime or cgroup path. Every later match uses these values. "Same minute as the rollout" does not count as a match.
- **l1i3** **Read the container's termination status first.** `lastState.terminated` (or the current `state.terminated`) gives `reason`, `exitCode`, and the start and finish times.
  - `reason: OOMKilled` means the runtime saw the cgroup OOM killer hit this container.
  - `Completed`, `Error`, or exit 143 means the process exited on SIGTERM or on its own.
  - Exit 137 without `OOMKilled` means the container got a SIGKILL from some source. Steps i4 and i5 identify which.
- **l1i4** **Look for an orchestrator stop.** Every record here must name the same pod UID.
  - The pod has a `deletionTimestamp`, or a `Killing` event says "Stopping container".
  - The API audit log shows a delete or eviction, and you can see who issued it: the ReplicaSet or Deployment controller during the rollout, a node drain, or a human.
  - The rollout's ReplicaSet scale-down history includes this pod.
  - The app log shows SIGTERM receipt or shutdown start.

  A SIGTERM followed by exit 137 at about `deletionTimestamp + terminationGracePeriodSeconds` is still an orchestrator stop. The worker simply didn't finish shutting down within the grace period.
- **l1i5** **Look for a memory kill.** There are two kinds, and they leave different records.
  - **Cgroup OOM:** the node's kernel log (`dmesg` or journal) has a `Memory cgroup out of memory: Killed process <PID>` line whose PID and cgroup path match the IDs from i2. The container cgroup's `memory.events` shows `oom_kill` incremented. Memory metrics should show the worker climbing toward its limit beforehand.
  - **Kubelet node-pressure eviction:** the pod shows `reason: Evicted` and an event citing memory pressure. In this case the orchestrator deleted the pod because the *node* was short on memory. It was not the kernel hitting the container's limit.
- **l1i6** **Decide on sequence when both trails exist.** If a `deletionTimestamp` precedes an OOM kill inside the grace window, the rollout initiated the stop and the OOM ended it. That usually means shutdown allocates heavily, which is a separate bug. If the OOM precedes any deletion, the memory kill is the cause and the rollout timing is coincidental.

**l2** The cause stays unresolved under any of these conditions:

- **l2i1** **The pod object is gone and its events have expired.** Kubernetes events default to a 1-hour TTL, and the replaced pod's status leaves with it. Without an audit log or an event exporter, nothing remains to show a deletion.
- **l2i2** **The node-side records are gone.** If the node was replaced, recycled, or rebooted, or the kernel ring buffer rotated and the journal isn't persisted, no OOM line exists to confirm or rule out a memory kill.
- **l2i3** **The only surviving evidence is exit 137 plus timing.** That fits both a grace-period SIGKILL and an OOM kill, so the cause stays a hypothesis. Operations' suggestion is in this category until a kernel OOM line or `OOMKilled` status matching the worker's identity turns up.
- **l2i4** **Records exist but can't be tied to this worker.** For example, an OOM line exists for a PID or cgroup you can't map to its container ID, or memory metrics were scraped too coarsely to show the climb.

The missing terminal record doesn't decide anything on its own. A SIGKILL'd process can't write one, but a gracefully stopped pod can also lose its final log lines if the log shipper didn't flush before the pod was removed.

The core problem is that a rollout and an OOM kill can both end in SIGKILL and exit code 137. The exit code alone won't settle it. You need a record that names the cause and is tied to the same container instance. Here's the walk-through assuming Kubernetes; other orchestrators use the same signals under different names.

**l1** Records to collect, matched on container ID, pod UID or PID first, and timestamp second:

- **l1i1** **Orchestrator side.**
  - The rollout's ReplicaSet scale-down and the pod's `deletionTimestamp`.
  - The API audit log entry for the pod DELETE, showing which controller or user issued it.
  - Pod events: `Killing` / "Stopping container", and preStop hook results.

  These establish that a stop was *requested* and when the grace period started.
- **l1i2** **Kernel side.** On the node that hosted the container, check `journalctl -k` or `dmesg` for "Memory cgroup out of memory: Killed process <PID> (<name>)". The cgroup path in that line contains the container ID. On cgroup v2, `memory.events` `oom_kill` also counts kills, but it disappears with the cgroup.
- **l1i3** **Runtime/kubelet side.**
  - containerd/CRI-O and kubelet logs for the container exit: exit code, `reason: OOMKilled` vs `Error`/`Completed`, and `finishedAt`.
  - Kubelet eviction messages, if node memory pressure triggered an eviction rather than a cgroup OOM.
- **l1i4** **Worker's own logs.** A SIGTERM handler or "shutting down" line is proof the orchestrator's signal arrived. It also shows whether the worker was still alive afterwards.
- **l1i5** **Memory metrics.** Look at the container working set against its limit in the minutes before death. This supports or weakens the OOM hypothesis. It never proves it, because scrape intervals miss the final spike.

**l2** How to decide:

- **l2i1** **Orchestrator stop.** You have a deletion request, followed by SIGTERM, and then an exit inside the grace period.
  - Exit 143 (or 0 with a clean shutdown) means the worker honoured the stop.
  - Exit 137 at `deletionTimestamp + terminationGracePeriodSeconds` means a grace-period SIGKILL: still an orchestrator stop, just a slow shutdown. There will be no kernel OOM line.
- **l2i2** **Memory kill.** You have a kernel OOM line whose cgroup or PID matches *this* container, and/or `reason: OOMKilled`.
  - If it happened before any deletion request, the OOM is the cause and the rollout timing is coincidence.
  - If it happened after SIGTERM, both occurred: the stop was requested, and the worker died of memory during shutdown. Report it that way rather than picking one.
- **l2i3** **Wrong process.** An OOM line naming a child process (e.g. an image-decoding subprocess) is not a kill of the worker. Check whether the worker exited afterwards or was stopped separately.

**l3** What leaves it unresolved:

- **l3i1** **Pod object deleted.** Its `lastState` went with it, and nothing else captured the termination reason. This is likely why the terminal record is "missing".
- **l3i2** **Events expired.** Events default to about 1 hour retention, and no audit logging was enabled.
- **l3i3** **Kernel and runtime logs gone.** The node was drained or replaced (rollouts and autoscalers do this), or its logs rotated before collection.
- **l3i4** **No matching identifier.** You can't match the kernel line's PID or cgroup to the container, only to the time window. That is correlation, not cause. The same applies to "it died right after the rollout".
- **l3i5** **Clock skew.** Skew between nodes and the control plane can blur the ordering when deletion and OOM land within seconds of each other.
- **l3i6** **Unrecorded killer.** A userspace OOM killer (systemd-oomd, earlyoom) logs to its own unit, not to the kernel ring buffer, so the kernel check alone comes up empty.

If you reach any of l3i1–l3i6 without a decisive record, the answer is "cause not established." It is not "probably OOM because Operations said so."

**f1** Check whether the worker is actually gone before you reconstruct its death. A rollout replaces pods with new names. If the dashboard is keyed on pod name or instance ID, a healthy replacement can look like a disappearance.

Timing next to a rollout doesn't establish the cause. "Missing terminal record" also only means the worker didn't log its own death, which is normal for both a SIGKILL and an OOM kill. You have to decide this from records outside the worker.

**l1** Records to collect, keyed to the exact worker instance (pod/container ID, node, host PID, cgroup path) rather than the service name:
- **i1** Orchestrator records: rollout history, controller events for scale-down or replacement of that instance, deletion timestamp, and the agent's "stopping/killing container" event. On Kubernetes, these are the ReplicaSet scale events, the pod's `deletionTimestamp`, and kubelet `Killing` events.
- **i2** Container runtime state: exit code, termination reason, and start and finish times. On Kubernetes this is `lastState.terminated` (`reason`, `exitCode`, `finishedAt`).
- **i3** Kernel records from the node: `dmesg` or `journalctl -k` lines like `Memory cgroup out of memory: Killed process <pid> (<name>)`, plus the `oom_kill` counter in the cgroup's `memory.events`.
- **i4** Memory metrics for that container in the minutes before it died: working set or RSS against its limit.
- **i5** The dashboard's own data: when the worker's last heartbeat or registration arrived, and whether a replacement instance registered under a new ID.

**l2** How to match them:
- **i1** Confirm it actually died. If a replacement registered under a new identity and the dashboard is keyed on the old one, this is a dashboard problem, not a kill.
- **i2** Orchestrator stop: a stop or delete event for that exact instance comes first. SIGTERM follows, then exit. Exit code 143 means it handled SIGTERM. Exit code 137 means SIGKILL, and here it should land almost exactly one grace period after the stop event. There should be no kernel OOM line for that PID. Memory should be below the limit.
- **i3** Memory kill: a kernel OOM line names the worker's PID inside its cgroup, and the `oom_kill` counter went up. The runtime reports `OOMKilled` with 137, and the exit time matches the kernel timestamp to within clock skew. Memory was at or near the limit. There's no preceding stop event, or one exists but comes after the kill (the rollout replacing a pod that was already dead).
- **i4** Don't treat 137 as evidence of OOM on its own. Grace-period expiry produces 137 too. The kernel OOM line, `memory.events`, or the runtime's `OOMKilled` reason is what separates the two.

**l3** What leaves the cause unresolved:
- **i1** The records have expired or are gone. Kubernetes events default to about a one-hour TTL. If the rollout also replaced or drained the node, its kernel ring buffer and journal may be gone with it.
- **i2** No record ties to the instance. For example, there's an OOM line but its PID or cgroup can't be matched to the worker, or the runtime record was garbage-collected.
- **i3** Both causes are present. A stop event came first, then the worker OOM'd while draining during its grace period. That is a real overlap. Report it as an OOM triggered during the orchestrated shutdown, not as either cause alone.
- **i4** You have exit code 137 with no OOM evidence and no stop event at the matching offset. That shows a SIGKILL from an unidentified sender, such as a manual kill, a node-level eviction, or a sidecar.
- **i5** The gap between events is smaller than clock skew between the node, the control plane, and the dashboard, so their order can't be established.

If you land in any of those, the honest conclusion is "SIGKILL or exit of unknown origin; memory kill unconfirmed," not Ops' guess restated with more confidence.

**f1** A missing page‑3 receipt doesn't mean page 3 is untouched. The run that stopped could have applied some page‑3 payments before it died, and that would leave no receipt. The receipt ledger tells you which pages finished, not which payments were applied.

**d2** Check every page‑3 payment against the payment store, using whatever key identifies a payment independently of the import run, such as the payment ID or external reference. **The write**

**a1** Submit page 3 by itself, exactly once.

**After the write**

- A page‑3 receipt exists.
- Every page‑3 payment is present exactly once.
- Count and total match d4.
- Page 1 and 2 counts are unchanged from d4.

**a2** Don't retry yet. First check whether a page‑3 receipt exists. If it does, the write succeeded, so run d5.

**a3** If there's no receipt, repeat d2 against the payment store:
- **No page‑3 payments present:** the write didn't happen. Repeat d3, then a1.
- **Some or all present:** page 3 is partially applied, or fully applied without a receipt. Do not resubmit page 3.

**l1** Recovery plan for page 3. It relies on one fact: a missing receipt does not prove page 3 wrote nothing. The importer writes the receipt only after the whole page is applied, so a crash partway through page 3 leaves some payments with no receipt.

**l1i1** Before the run, stop anything else that might write. Confirm no importer process, scheduled job or automatic retry is still active, so nothing can apply page 3 while you check or after you run it.

**l1i2** Before the run, confirm the receipt ledger. It should show receipts for pages 1 and 2 and none for page 3. If page 3 already has a receipt, stop: it is done, and running it again duplicates it.

**l1i3** Before the run, check whether any page-3 payments already exist. Look up each one in the destination by a stable key, such as a source payment ID or reference. Do not use amount or date alone, because those can match unrelated payments. Branch on the result:
- None exist: proceed.
- All exist: page 3 was applied but its receipt was not written. Do not rerun it. Record the gap and reconcile the receipt.
- Some exist: do not run the full page, because it would duplicate those payments. Go to l1i7.

**l1i4** Before the run, take a baseline. Record the destination's payment count and total amount for the scope page 3 affects, along with page 3's own payment count and total. The post-run check uses these numbers.

**l1i5** Run page 3 exactly once, as a single-page import. Capture the full output and exit status.

**l1i6** After the run, verify three things:
- The receipt ledger has a page-3 receipt.
- Every page-3 payment exists exactly once, checked by its key.
- The destination count and total increased by exactly page 3's count and total compared with the baseline. A larger increase means duplicates; a smaller one means missing payments.

Pages 1 and 2 should show no new duplicates.

**l1i7** If a write's outcome is uncertain, do not retry blindly. A timeout, crash, lost connection or ambiguous exit status gets the same treatment:
1. Confirm no process is still running the write.
2. Repeat l1i2 and l1i3 against current state.
3. Act on what you find:
   - A receipt exists: it succeeded. Run the l1i6 checks.
   - No payments exist: nothing landed, so retry once.
   - All payments exist but no receipt: it succeeded, but the receipt is missing. Do not rerun.
   - Some payments exist: this is a partial apply. Rerunning the page duplicates the ones that already landed.

**l1i8** A partial apply has two possible repairs, and your facts don't establish which one is safe:
- Run only the missing payments. This works only if the importer accepts a hand-built page containing just those payments, and if that won't confuse receipt tracking for page 3.
- Remove the page-3 payments that did land, then run the full page. This is destructive, so check downstream effects such as reconciliations, notifications and posted balances first.

Either way, find out how the receipt for page 3 gets written. Otherwise the ledger and the payments will disagree.

**f1** The plan depends on page-3 payments carrying a stable key you can look up. Nothing you've described confirms that they do. If they don't, check l1i3 by hand against the source file, and treat any page-3 failure as needing a manual reconciliation rather than a retry.

Publish Manifest

Explain our static-site release process to a new teammate. We upload all new assets under versioned names, then switch the manifest to those names. Old assets stay available for browsers that already fetched the previous manifest. Explain why the upload precedes the switch and why we keep the old assets.

Baseline · repetition 1 · Automatic pass · 190 words

Blind review · Missed
The lazy-loading example explains retention well, but the stated process does not establish an atomic release for every visitor. The final paragraph repeats the point that versioned files can coexist.

Each release ships in two steps: first we upload every new asset under a versioned name, such as `app.4f2c.js`, and then we update the manifest to point at those names.

The upload comes before the switch so the manifest never references a file that doesn't exist yet. Once the manifest changes, any browser can fetch it and immediately request the new asset names. If those files aren't already in place, that browser gets 404s and a broken page. Because the files are already there when the switch happens, the release takes effect atomically: a visitor gets either the complete old version or the complete new one.

We keep the old assets because the switch doesn't reach browsers that already have the previous manifest. A page opened before the release will still request old asset names, for example when lazy-loading a chunk or navigating. If we deleted those files, those sessions would break partway through. Keeping the old assets lets every browser finish with the version it started on.

Versioned names are what make both steps safe. New files never overwrite old ones, so both versions can sit side by side.
Candidate · repetition 1 · Automatic pass · 255 words

Blind review · Missed
It explains both reasons but assumes the manifest is the browser’s only source of filenames and that all new names are requested immediately. It repeats the no-overwrite point and introduces indefinite caching beyond the request.

A release has two steps, in this order: upload every new asset under a versioned name, then switch the manifest to point at those names. Old assets are never deleted as part of the release.

**Why upload comes first:** The manifest is the only thing that tells a browser which files to load. Once it changes, any browser that fetches it will immediately request the new names. If those files aren't uploaded yet, those requests 404 and the page breaks. Uploading first guarantees that every name the new manifest mentions already exists. Because the new files have new names, uploading them doesn't touch anything the live site uses. The only step users can see is the manifest switch, which happens in one step.

**Why old assets stay:** Switching the manifest doesn't update browsers that already loaded the old one. A tab opened before the release still holds the old manifest and will keep requesting old asset names as it lazy-loads routes, chunks, images, or fonts. If those files were gone, a user in the middle of a session would get broken pages until they reloaded. Keeping the old files lets both versions work at the same time. Users already on the site keep the release they started with, and new visitors get the new one.

The versioned names are what make this safe. Each release's files sit at their own names, so the two releases never overwrite each other, and caches can hold any asset indefinitely because a given name always means the same content.

A release has two steps: upload every new asset under a versioned name, then switch the manifest to point at those names.

The upload comes first so the manifest never references a file that doesn't exist yet. If we switched first, any browser that fetched the new manifest before the uploads finished would request missing assets and get a broken page. Once every versioned file is already in place, the switch is safe at any moment.

We keep the old assets because some browsers already loaded the previous manifest and will keep requesting the files it lists, sometimes long after the switch. Because every version has its own filenames, the old files can stay alongside the new ones without conflict. Those browsers keep working until they pick up the new manifest.
Candidate · repetition 2 · Automatic pass · 209 words

Blind review · Missed
Both reasons are clear, but asset availability alone does not guarantee that every browser always sees a consistent set of files. The opening and numbered overview repeat points developed under the two headings.

Our releases are ordered so that every browser always sees a consistent set of files, whichever version it loaded.

**How it works**

1. Upload every new asset under a versioned name. Because each version gets its own names, the upload never overwrites anything the live site uses.
2. Switch the manifest to point at the new names. This one change is the release.
3. Leave the old assets in place.

**Why the upload comes first**

A browser that fetches the new manifest immediately requests the files it names. If we switched the manifest first, those requests could reach files that hadn't finished uploading and fail, breaking the page for anyone who loaded during that window. Uploading first means every file the new manifest references already exists the moment the manifest goes live. Until then, the new files sit unused alongside the live ones.

**Why we keep the old assets**

The switch doesn't reach browsers that already fetched the previous manifest. They keep requesting the old names. If we deleted those files at release time, those users would get failed requests even though nothing was wrong on their end. Keeping the old assets lets them carry on with the version they started on, while new visitors get the new one.

Our release has two steps in a fixed order: upload every new asset under a versioned name, then switch the manifest to point at those names. Old assets are never deleted during a release.

**Why the upload comes first:** The manifest is what browsers use to find assets. Once it changes, any browser that loads it immediately requests the files it names. If those files aren't uploaded yet, the browser gets 404s and the page breaks. Uploading first means every file the new manifest references already exists when the switch happens. Because the new files have new, versioned names, uploading them doesn't affect anyone on the current release. Nothing references them until the manifest changes. This makes the manifest switch the single moment the release takes effect. If the upload fails partway, we stop, and users see no change.

**Why we keep the old assets:** A browser that loaded the previous manifest keeps requesting the files it named. This happens with lazy-loaded chunks, a later navigation in a single-page app, or a tab left open for hours. If we deleted those files at the switch, those users would get 404s in the middle of a session, even though nothing on their side is wrong. Keeping the old assets lets every client finish on the version it started with and pick up the new one on its next manifest fetch. It also makes rollback simple: point the manifest back at the previous names, and those files are still there.

**Why the versioned names matter:** Each release's files have their own names, so the new upload never overwrites a file that a live client might be fetching. The same names also let us cache assets aggressively. A given URL always serves the same bytes.

Every release goes out in two steps, and the order matters.

**1. Upload the new assets under versioned names.** Each changed file (JS bundles, CSS, images) gets a name that includes its version or content hash, such as `app.3f9c2a.js`. Nothing references these files yet, so uploading them has no effect on what users see.

**2. Switch the manifest to the new names.** The manifest (or the HTML that loads the assets) is the only file that tells a browser which asset names to request. Updating it is the moment the release goes live.

**Why the upload happens first:** As soon as the manifest changes, browsers start requesting the names it lists. If those files aren't uploaded yet, users get 404s, which can mean a blank page, missing styles or broken scripts. Uploading first means every name the new manifest points to already exists when the switch happens. It also makes the switch a single change to one file, so the release goes live in one step instead of piece by piece.

**Why the old assets stay available:** A browser that loaded the previous manifest keeps using those older asset names, sometimes for a long time. Open tabs, back/forward cache, CDN or proxy caches, and service workers can all keep serving the old manifest. Many apps also load scripts and chunks lazily, for example when a user navigates to a new route. If the old files were deleted, those users would hit 404s in the middle of a session even though nothing is wrong on their end. Keeping the old assets lets every client finish with the version it started on, and the next full page load picks up the new manifest.

Keeping the old files also makes rollback cheap: pointing the manifest back at the previous names restores the previous release with nothing to re-upload.

Explain our static-site release process to a new teammate. We upload all new assets under versioned names, then switch the manifest to those names. Our releases happen in two steps: first we upload every new asset under a versioned name, then we switch the manifest to point at those new names. The old assets stay where they are.

The upload comes first so the manifest never points at files that aren't there yet. If we switched the manifest first, any browser that fetched it before the upload finished would request new asset names that don't exist yet and get broken pages. Uploading first means that by the time anyone can see the new names, every file behind them is already in place. Versioned names make this safe: the new files sit alongside the old ones without overwriting anything, so uploading them has no effect on live traffic until the switch.

We keep the old assets because switching the manifest doesn't update browsers that already loaded the previous one. Those browsers still hold the old names and will keep requesting those files. If we deleted them, those users would hit missing files partway through their session. Keeping the old assets lets every browser finish with the set it started with, while new visitors get the new release.

The upload comes first so that the manifest never references a file that doesn't exist yet. As soon as the manifest switches, browsers start requesting whatever names it lists. If any of those assets were still uploading, those requests would fail and pages would break. Uploading everything first means that when the switch happens, every file it names is already in place.

We keep the old assets because some browsers already fetched the previous manifest and will keep requesting the files it named. Deleting those files would break pages for those users even though they did nothing wrong. Versioned names let the old and new sets coexist without colliding, so both the old and new manifests stay fully served.

Each release uploads every new asset under a versioned name, such as `app.3f9c2a.js`, before anything references it. Only then do we switch the manifest to point at the new names.

**Why the upload comes first:** The manifest tells browsers which files to load. If we switched it before the uploads finished, a browser could fetch the new manifest and then request files that don't exist yet. That browser would get 404s and a broken page. Uploading first means every name in the new manifest already resolves when the switch happens, so the switch is effectively atomic.

**Why we keep the old assets:** Some browsers fetched the previous manifest before the switch, from an open tab or a cached copy. They will keep requesting the old versioned files. If we deleted those files, those users would hit missing scripts or styles partway through a session. Because versioned names never collide, the old and new sets can live side by side. Each browser gets a complete, consistent set of files, whichever manifest it loaded.

Our release has two steps: upload every new asset under a new versioned filename (e.g. `app.3f9c2.js`), then update the manifest so pages point at those new names.

The upload comes first so the manifest never references a file that doesn't exist yet. If we switched the manifest first, any browser that loaded it before the upload finished would request the new filenames, get 404s, and render a broken page. Uploading first means the moment the manifest flips, everything it points to is already in place.

We keep the old assets because switching the manifest doesn't update browsers that already have the previous one. A user mid-session, or one with a cached page, still requests the old filenames, sometimes lazily, minutes later. If we deleted those files on release, those users would hit 404s for scripts, styles or chunks their page expects. Leaving them available lets the old version keep working until those sessions naturally move to the new manifest.

The versioned names are what make both steps safe. New files never overwrite old ones, so the two versions coexist and the manifest switch is the only thing that decides which one a fresh visitor gets.

A release has two steps: we upload every new asset under a versioned name, then we switch the manifest to point at those names.

The upload comes first so the manifest never references a file that isn't there yet. As soon as the manifest switches, browsers start requesting the names it lists. If we switched first, those requests could hit missing files and the page would break until the upload caught up. Because the new names are versioned, uploading them early doesn't touch anything the live manifest uses, so it's safe to do while the old release is still serving.

We keep the old assets because some browsers fetched the previous manifest before the switch and will keep requesting the old names it listed. If we deleted those files at the switch, those browsers would get failures partway through loading. Leaving the old versions in place lets both manifests resolve completely, so the switch is safe for everyone, whichever manifest they loaded.

A release happens in two steps. First we upload every new asset under a versioned name, so it never overwrites an existing file. Then we switch the manifest so it points to those new names.

The upload comes before the switch so the manifest never points at a file that doesn't exist yet. Once the manifest changes, browsers start requesting the new names immediately. If those files were still uploading, users would get 404s and broken pages. Uploading first means every name in the new manifest is already live when the switch happens.

We keep the old assets because some browsers already fetched the previous manifest and will keep requesting the files it lists, such as a tab that was open during the release. If we deleted those files, those users would hit missing scripts and styles partway through their session. Versioned names let both sets of files exist side by side, so old and new manifests each resolve to a complete, consistent set of assets.

The upload comes first because the manifest is what sends browsers to assets. If we switched the manifest first, a browser could fetch it and request a versioned file that hasn't been uploaded yet, and that request would fail. The switch then works as a single cutover from fully available old assets to fully available new ones.

We keep the old assets because switching the manifest doesn't update browsers that already have the previous one. Those browsers will keep requesting the old versioned names. Because each release uses new names, the old files never conflict with the new ones, so keeping them serves those browsers at no risk to the new release.

The upload comes first because the manifest is what tells browsers which files to load. If we switched it before the files were in place, any browser that fetched the new manifest in that gap would request assets that don't exist yet and get a broken page. Uploading first means every name the new manifest references is already servable when the manifest goes live, so the switch itself is the single moment the release takes effect.

The examples explain both reasons, but uploading first establishes asset availability. It does not establish that the manifest switch itself is atomic.

When we release, we first upload every new asset under a versioned name, such as `app.3f9c2.js`, and only then switch the manifest to point at those new names. Old assets stay where they are.

**Why the upload comes first:** the manifest switch is the moment browsers start asking for the new files. If we switched first, any browser that fetched the new manifest before the uploads finished would request files that don't exist yet. That means broken pages, missing styles, or failed scripts. Uploading first means every name in the new manifest already resolves by the time anyone can see it, so the switch is effectively atomic.

**Why we keep the old assets:** a browser that loaded the previous manifest will keep requesting the asset names it lists, for example when it lazy-loads a chunk or navigates within an already-open page. If we deleted those files at release, those users would get 404s mid-session. Because versioned names never collide, the old and new sets can sit side by side. Each browser gets a consistent set of files matching the manifest it actually has.

A release has two steps: upload every new asset under a versioned name (e.g. `app.3f9c.js`), then switch the manifest to point at those names. The manifest is the only thing that decides which assets a page loads, so the switch is the moment the release goes live.

**Why the upload comes first:** once the manifest is switched, any browser that fetches it will immediately request the new names. If those files weren't already uploaded, those requests would fail and users would get a broken page. Uploading first means every name the new manifest references already exists when it goes live. Because the new files have new names, uploading them can't affect anyone still on the old manifest.

**Why we keep the old assets:** browsers that fetched the previous manifest before the switch will keep requesting the old names, for example when lazy-loading a chunk or loading the next page. If we deleted the old files at switch time, those requests would fail mid-session. Leaving the old assets in place lets those browsers finish on the old version while new visitors get the new one.

Publish Manifest

Explain our static-site release process to a new teammate. We upload all new assets under versioned names, then switch the manifest to those names. Old assets stay available for browsers that already fetched the previous manifest. Explain why the upload precedes the switch and why we keep the old assets.

Baseline · repetition 1 · Automatic pass · 180 words

Blind review · Missed
Browsers may defer asset requests, and switching the manifest does not move existing visitors to the new release in one step. The closing claim about correctness adds a broader assurance after the retention reason is already clear.

A release has two steps: upload every new asset under a new versioned name (for example `app.3f9c2.js`), then switch the manifest so it points at those names.

The upload comes first because the manifest switch is what makes a release live. Once a browser fetches the new manifest, it immediately requests the files it names. If those files weren't already uploaded, the browser would get 404s and render a broken page. Uploading first means every name the new manifest references already exists, so switching the manifest moves visitors from one complete release to another in a single step.

We keep the old assets because switching the manifest doesn't update browsers that already loaded the previous one. Those pages still request the old versioned names, for example when they lazy-load a chunk or fetch an image later in the session. If we deleted the old files at release time, those users would hit missing files partway through their visit. Because every release uses new names, the old files never conflict with the new ones, so keeping them costs nothing in correctness.

Each release has two steps. First, upload every new asset under a versioned name, such as `app.3f9c2a.js`, alongside the existing files. Then update the manifest so it points to those new names. Browsers load the manifest to find out which files to request.

The upload comes first so that every file the new manifest names already exists when a browser reads it. If we switched first, a browser could fetch the new manifest and then request files that haven't finished uploading. It would get 404s and show a broken page. Uploading first means a browser sees either the complete old set or the complete new set, never a mix.

We keep the old assets because switching the manifest doesn't update browsers that already loaded the previous one. A page opened before the release keeps requesting the old names as it lazy-loads scripts, styles, images and route chunks. If those files were deleted, those users would hit errors partway through their session. Because each version uses distinct names, old and new files can coexist without overwriting each other.

A release happens in two steps. First, we upload every new asset under a versioned name, such as `app.3f9c2a.js` instead of `app.js`. Then we switch the manifest so it points to those new names. Each version gets its own filenames, so a release never overwrites a file that someone might still be loading.

The upload happens before the switch because the manifest is what sends browsers to the new files. If we switched it first, some browsers would read the new manifest and request files that haven't been uploaded yet, which would fail. We keep the old assets because browsers don't all move to the new manifest at the same moment. A browser that loaded the previous manifest, whether from an open tab or a cache, will keep requesting the old filenames, often to load more of the page. If we deleted those files, those pages would break partway through. Leaving the old versions in place lets every browser finish with the version it started on and pick up the new one on its next manifest fetch.

Publish Manifest

Explain our static-site release process to a new teammate. We upload all new assets under versioned names, then switch the manifest to those names. Old assets stay available for browsers that already fetched the previous manifest. Explain why the upload precedes the switch and why we keep the old assets.

Baseline · repetition 1 · Automatic pass · 152 words

Blind review · Missed
Covers both reasons, but a browser can defer asset requests. Upload order ensures the referenced files exist and does not establish that manifest publication is atomic.

A release has two steps: upload every new asset under a versioned name, then switch the manifest to point at those names.

The upload comes first because the manifest is what browsers follow. Once it changes, any browser that loads it immediately requests the new names. If those files weren't already uploaded, the browser would get 404s and a broken page. Uploading first means every name the new manifest references already exists when the manifest goes live, so the switch is effectively atomic.

We keep the old assets because the switch doesn't reach browsers that already fetched the previous manifest. Those pages still request the old names, for example when lazy-loading a chunk or fetching an image later in the session. Deleting the old files would break those users mid-session. Since every release uses new versioned names, old and new files never collide, so both can be served at the same time.

Uploading first means every name the new manifest mentions already exists when the switch happens. The switch then becomes the single moment the release goes live.

The old assets stay because some browsers already fetched the previous manifest and will keep requesting the files it names. Since every release uses new versioned names, the old files aren't overwritten, so those browsers keep getting a consistent set of files. Delete the old files and those browsers break until they pick up the new manifest.

The upload comes first because the manifest is what tells browsers which files to load. If we switched it before the upload finished, a browser could fetch the new manifest and then request files that aren't there yet, which breaks the page. Uploading first means every name in the new manifest already resolves when it goes live.

We keep the old assets because some browsers fetched the previous manifest before the switch and will keep requesting the files it names. Deleting those files would break pages for those users mid-session. Leaving them in place lets those browsers finish with the old version while new visitors get the new one.
Candidate · repetition 2 · Automatic pass · 216 words

Blind review · Missed
The claim that the browser has no way to recover is unsupported. The reply repeats the file-availability point, and the aside about users doing nothing wrong adds no release detail.

A release has two steps. First, we upload every new asset under a versioned name, so nothing already live gets overwritten. Then we switch the manifest to point at those new names. The old assets stay where they are.

**Why the upload comes first:** The manifest is what tells browsers which files to load. If we switched it before the uploads finished, a browser could fetch the new manifest and then request files that don't exist yet. That means broken pages, missing styles or scripts, and no way to fix it from the browser's side. With the upload first, every name the new manifest mentions already exists when the switch happens. The switch becomes the single moment the release goes live, and anyone who loads it gets a complete set of files.

**Why we keep the old assets:** Some browsers fetched the previous manifest before the switch and will keep asking for the files it lists. If we deleted those files, those users would get failed requests in the middle of a session, even though they did nothing wrong. Because the new assets use different names, the old ones never get in the way. Both versions can be served at the same time, and each browser gets a consistent set that matches the manifest it has.

Our releases happen in two steps. First, we upload every new asset (JS, CSS, images and so on) under a versioned filename, so new files never overwrite existing ones. Second, we update the manifest to point at those new names. Old assets stay where they are.

**Why the upload comes first:** The manifest is what tells a browser which files to load. Once it points at the new names, any browser that fetches it will immediately request those files. If they aren't uploaded yet, those requests fail and users get a broken or unstyled page. Uploading first means every file the new manifest references already exists when the switch happens, so the switch takes effect for everyone at once.

**Why we keep the old assets:** Browsers that loaded the previous manifest before the switch still hold references to the old filenames. They keep requesting those files as they navigate or lazy-load parts of the page. If we deleted the old assets at release time, those users would hit missing files partway through a session. Keeping the old assets lets those sessions finish on the version they started with, while new visitors get the new release.

Publish Manifest

Explain our static-site release process to a new teammate. We upload all new assets under versioned names, then switch the manifest to those names. Old assets stay available for browsers that already fetched the previous manifest. Explain why the upload precedes the switch and why we keep the old assets.

Baseline · repetition 1 · Automatic pass · 287 words

Blind review · Missed
Both reasons are present, but the process does not guarantee that users never see mixed versions or that caches can never serve stale files. The rollback procedure is unsolicited, and the closing paragraph repeats the upload rationale.

Each release happens in two steps, and the order matters.

1. **Upload every new asset under a versioned name.** Each file gets a name that changes whenever its content changes, such as `app.3f9c2a.js`. Nothing references these files yet, so uploading them changes nothing users see.
2. **Switch the manifest to the new names.** The manifest tells browsers which asset files make up the current site. Changing it is the single step that releases the new version.

**Why the upload comes first:** once the manifest changes, any browser that loads it will immediately request the files it names. If any of those files are still uploading, the browser gets 404s and the page breaks or renders partly. Uploading first means every file the new manifest references already exists when the manifest goes live. Because the manifest switch is a single change, users get either the complete old version or the complete new one, never a mix.

**Why we keep the old assets:** a browser that loaded the previous manifest before the switch still has those references. It will keep requesting the old files when it lazy-loads a route, fetches a chunk, or retries after a cache eviction. That can happen minutes or hours later in a long-lived tab. If we deleted the old files at release time, those users would hit 404s mid-session. Keeping the old files lets every session finish on the version it started with. It also makes rollback cheap: point the manifest back at the previous names, and nothing needs to be re-uploaded.

Versioned names make both steps safe. New files never overwrite old ones, so uploading can't disturb the live site, and a cache can never serve a stale file under a current name.

A release has two steps: upload every new asset under a versioned name, then switch the manifest to point at those names. Old assets are never overwritten and stay online afterward.

**Why the upload comes first:** The manifest switch is the moment users start receiving the new release. Once a browser loads the new manifest, it immediately requests the files the manifest names. If any of those files were still uploading, the request would return a 404 or a partial file, and the page would break or render without styles or scripts. Uploading everything first means every name in the new manifest already resolves when the switch happens. The switch then flips the whole release at once instead of exposing a half-deployed state. If the upload fails partway, nothing user-facing has changed, and you can simply retry.

**Why the old assets are kept:** Browsers that loaded the page before the switch still hold the previous manifest. They keep requesting the old names as they lazy-load chunks, navigate within the app, or fetch images. CDN and browser caches may also serve the old manifest for a while after the switch. If the old files were deleted, those sessions would hit missing assets mid-use. Versioned names are what make keeping them possible: new files never overwrite old ones, so both releases can be served side by side. The same property makes rollback cheap. Pointing the manifest back at the previous names restores the prior release with no re-upload.

**Why the old assets stay.** Switching the manifest doesn't update browsers that are already running. A page loaded a minute before the release still holds the old manifest and will keep requesting old asset names, for example when it lazy-loads a route chunk, fetches a font, or recovers from a dropped request. Because each name is unique to its content, old and new files never collide, and CDN and browser caches never serve a stale file under a current name.

Publish Manifest

Explain our static-site release process to a new teammate. We upload all new assets under versioned names, then switch the manifest to those names. Old assets stay available for browsers that already fetched the previous manifest. Explain why the upload precedes the switch and why we keep the old assets.

Baseline · repetition 1 · Automatic pass · 243 words

Blind review · Missed
The process does not establish that every browser fetching the manifest during an early switch would request an unfinished file, or that every new page load picks up the new manifest. The final paragraph repeats the opening point about avoiding overwrites.

Each release has two steps. First we upload every new asset under a versioned name. Then we switch the manifest so it points to those names. We never overwrite or delete the previous release's assets as part of the release.

**Why upload comes first:** The manifest is what tells browsers which files to load. If we switched it before the new files existed, any browser that fetched the new manifest in that gap would request files that aren't there. The result is broken pages, missing styles, or scripts that fail. Uploading first means every name in the new manifest already resolves when the manifest goes live. The switch is then a single change from one complete release to another.

**Why we keep old assets:** Browsers don't all move to the new release at the same moment. Someone who loaded the page a minute before the switch still has the old manifest. As they navigate or lazy-load code, they'll keep requesting the old versioned files. If those files were gone, that user's session would break partway through, even though nothing was wrong with either release. Leaving the old assets available lets in-flight sessions finish on the release they started with. New page loads pick up the new manifest naturally.

Versioned names are what make both steps safe. Because new files never reuse an old name, uploading them can't disturb the live release, and old and new can coexist without either one overwriting the other.

Blind review · Missed

Our releases happen in two steps: first we upload every new asset under a versioned name, then we switch the manifest to point at those names. Old assets stay in place after the switch.

**Why the upload comes first:** The manifest is what browsers use to find assets. As soon as it changes, browsers start requesting the new names. If the manifest switched before the upload finished, those requests would hit files that don't exist yet, and the page would break. Uploading first means every name in the new manifest already resolves when it goes live. Versioned names make this safe: the new files can't overwrite anything the current release is using, so uploading them has no effect on live traffic until the switch.

**Why we keep the old assets:** A browser that loaded the previous manifest before the switch will keep requesting the old names for the rest of that session. If we deleted those files at release time, those users would get missing scripts, styles, or images partway through their visit. Keeping the old assets lets each browser finish with a consistent set of files from whichever release it started on.

Here's how a release works and why the steps are in this order.

When we release, we upload every new asset under a versioned name, so a new build never overwrites a file from the current one. Once everything is uploaded, we switch the manifest to point at the new names. That switch is the moment the release goes live.

**Why the upload comes first:** The manifest tells browsers which files to request. If we switched it before the uploads finished, any browser that fetched the new manifest would ask for files that don't exist yet and get errors, so the page would load broken. Uploading first means every file the new manifest names already exists when the manifest goes live. Until then, browsers keep using the old manifest and old files, which are untouched. Nobody sees a half-finished release.

**Why we keep the old assets:** Switching the manifest doesn't update browsers that already have the previous one, such as open tabs or pages loaded just before the release. Those browsers keep requesting the old names, for example when they load a file they hadn't needed yet. If we deleted the old assets, those requests would fail and the page would break for those users. Versioned names let both releases sit side by side without conflict. New visitors get the new files, and existing sessions keep working with the old ones.

The final claim that the switch alone decides which release a browser uses overlooks the manifest the browser already holds. The closing paragraph also repeats how the two releases coexist.

Our static-site releases happen in two steps: we upload every new asset under a versioned name, then we switch the manifest to point at those names. Old assets stay where they are.

**Why the upload comes first:** the manifest switch is the moment browsers start asking for the new names. If we switched before the upload finished, a browser could fetch the new manifest and then request an asset that doesn't exist yet. The result would be a broken page. Because the assets are already in place before the switch, every name the new manifest points to resolves from the first request.

**Why we keep the old assets:** a browser that loaded the page before the switch is still working from the previous manifest. It will keep requesting the old versioned names as it loads scripts, styles or images. If we deleted those files at release time, those users would hit missing assets mid-session. Keeping the old assets lets those browsers finish on the version they started with, while new visitors get the new one.

Versioned names are what make both steps safe. New files never overwrite old ones, so the old and new releases can be served side by side, and the manifest switch is the only thing that decides which release a browser uses.

Explain our static-site release process to a new teammate. We upload all new assets under versioned names, then switch the manifest to those names. Every release is two steps: upload the new assets under new versioned names, then point the manifest at them. The old assets stay up afterward.

**Why upload comes first:** The manifest switch is the moment users start getting the new release. If it happened before the upload, a browser could fetch the new manifest and then request assets that don't exist yet, giving it broken pages or missing scripts. Uploading first means every name the new manifest points to is already there when the manifest goes live. Because each version uses its own names, the upload doesn't touch anything the current release is serving.

**Why the old assets stay:** The switch doesn't reach browsers that already loaded the previous manifest. Those sessions keep requesting the old names, for example when they lazy-load a chunk or navigate to another page. If those files were deleted, those users would hit missing assets in the middle of a session. Keeping them available lets every browser finish with a consistent set of files from whichever release it started on.

The result is that no client ever sees a manifest pointing at files that aren't there, whether those files are new or old.

**Why we keep the old assets:** some browsers fetched the previous manifest before the switch and are still running from it. That manifest names the old files, so those browsers will keep requesting them. If we deleted the old files at release time, those users would hit missing assets partway through their session. Keeping the old files means both the previous and the current manifest work at the same time. Old sessions finish on the old version, and new sessions load the new one.

Versioned names are what make this possible. Old and new files never share a name, so they can sit side by side without overwriting each other.

Explain our static-site release process to a new teammate. We upload all new assets under versioned names, then switch the manifest to those names. Our static-site release has two steps, in a fixed order.

First, we upload every new asset under a versioned name, so a new file never overwrites an existing one. Second, we switch the manifest to point at the new names. The manifest is what tells a browser which asset files to load.

**Why the upload comes first:** the manifest switch is the moment a release goes live. Once it happens, any browser that fetches the manifest immediately requests the files it names. If we switched first, some of those files might not be uploaded yet, and those browsers would get missing assets and a broken page. Uploading first means every file the new manifest names already exists when anyone can see it. The switch becomes a single cutover, and nobody ever sees a half-released site.

**Why we keep the old assets:** a browser that loaded the previous manifest before the switch still holds the old file names and will keep requesting them for the rest of that session. If we deleted the old files at release time, those browsers would start failing in the middle of a session. Leaving them in place lets those visitors keep working on the old version until they next load the manifest and move to the new one. Because the names are versioned, both sets of files can sit side by side without conflict.

**Why the upload comes first:** The manifest switch is the moment browsers start asking for the new names. If any of those files weren't uploaded yet, browsers would get 404s and the page would break. Uploading first means every file the new manifest references already exists before anyone can see the manifest. Because the names are versioned, the upload doesn't overwrite anything the current site uses, so it's invisible to users until the switch. The switch itself is then the single step that changes what users get.

**Why we keep the old assets:** A browser that already fetched the previous manifest, such as an open tab, keeps requesting the old names, for example when it loads a chunk or image later in the session. If we deleted those files at release time, those users would hit 404s partway through using the site. Keeping them means each browser always gets a complete, matching set of files, either all old or all new, never a mix.

Because the versioned names differ, old and new assets can sit side by side without conflict, so keeping the old ones costs us nothing in correctness.
